orig_9709_s1_rep_stem_reading.description: Identify what each observation represents, organise every recorded value accurately, and use ordered positions to calculate the median and quartiles.

sections.title: What kind of data have I collected?
sections.label: Labels, counts and measurements
sections.intro: A variable is the property recorded for each individual or item. The individual records are the raw data. Classify what the values mean, rather than how they happen to be written.

blocks.html:
TypeMeaningExample
Qualitative, or categoricalA label or categoryFlower colour or an identification code
Quantitative and discreteA numerical quantity with separate possible valuesThe number of flowers on a plant
Quantitative and continuousAn underlying measurement that can take any value in an intervalThe height of a plant

A number used as a label is still categorical. Counts are discrete. For measurements, distinguish the continuous quantity from its rounded record: recording a height to the nearest centimetre does not turn the underlying height into a count.

blocks.title: Classify what the values mean
blocks.prompt: Classify each variable: a player’s shirt number used only to identify them; the number of books borrowed; and the actual length of a leaf, recorded to the nearest millimetre.

options.qualitative: Qualitative: the number is a label.

blocks.hint: Ask whether arithmetic on the numbers describes a real quantity, then distinguish counts from underlying measurements.
blocks.solution:
1. The shirt number is an identifier: adding or averaging such labels does not measure a property of the players. It is qualitative.

  2. The number of books is a count, so it is quantitative and discrete.

  3. The actual length is a measurement that can vary continuously. Rounding its recorded value does not make the underlying length discrete.

blocks.html: State the variable and explain the classification in context. “It is a number” is not enough: an identifier, a count and a measurement can all be written using digits.

sections.title: How do I construct and read a stem-and-leaf diagram?
sections.label: Place value, keys and split stems
sections.intro: A stem-and-leaf diagram displays individual numerical observations in order. The stem contains the leading digits, and each leaf is one final digit at a fixed place value. A key gives that place value and the units; the same pair of digits can represent different measurements under different keys.

blocks.html:
1. Choose a consistent stem and single-digit leaf from the recorded precision.
  2. List the stems in order, including empty stems within the displayed range.
  3. Enter one leaf for every observation, keeping all repetitions and zero leaves.
  4. Order the leaves on each row and write a key with units.
  5. Count the leaves to check that every observation appears once.
The key \(2\mid4=2.4\,\mathrm{cm}\) fixes the scale. Repeated leaves preserve repeated heights; stem \(4\) remains empty. The ordered positions also support the quartile method below.

If a row is crowded, split every stem into two rows: first leaves \(0\) to \(4\), then leaves \(5\) to \(9\). Label the groups clearly and use the same split throughout. Splitting changes the layout, not the recorded values or the number of observations.

blocks.title: Read a key, repeated leaves and an empty stem
blocks.prompt:
The diagram shows recorded task times.

StemLeaves
\(1\)\(3\quad5\quad5\quad8\)
\(2\)\(4\quad6\)
\(3\)
\(4\)\(1\)

Key: \(1\mid3\) means \(13\,\mathrm{s}\). Find the number of observations, the largest time and the repeated time. Interpret the empty stem.

options.none: No recorded time lies from \(30\) to \(39\) seconds.
options.zero: There is one time of \(30\) seconds.
options.missing: Some records must have been lost.

blocks.hint: Count leaves, including both copies of a repeated leaf. Read each leaf together with its stem and the key.
blocks.solution:
1. The ordered times are

    \[13,\ 15,\ 15,\ 18,\ 24,\ 26,\ 41.\]

  2. There are \(7\) observations. The largest is \(41\,\mathrm{s}\), and \(15\,\mathrm{s}\) occurs twice.

  3. The empty stem contributes no observation. A time of \(30\,\mathrm{s}\) would require a leaf \(0\) on stem \(3\).

blocks.html: An empty stem does not represent a value ending in zero. A value such as \(3.0\) must have its own zero leaf. Do not replace repeated leaves with a single copy: quartiles depend on the full ordered list.

sections.title: How do I find the median, quartiles and IQR?
sections.label: Ordered positions and medians of halves
sections.intro: Put the observations in increasing order and count all of them, including repeats. For odd \(n\), the median is the observation at position \(\frac{n+1}{2}\). For even \(n\), average the observations at positions \(\frac{n}{2}\) and \(\frac{n}{2}+1\). A position is not a data value.

blocks.html:
Convention used in this lesson: find \(Q_1\) as the median of the lower half and \(Q_3\) as the median of the upper half. When \(n\) is odd, exclude the single overall middle observation from both halves. When \(n\) is even, split all observations into two equal halves.

\[\mathrm{IQR}=Q_3-Q_1,\qquad\text{range}=x_{\max}-x_{\min}.\]

These measures of spread keep the units of the original data. Quartile conventions can differ between resources or software; use a rule explicitly supplied in the question. The raw-data exercises here state the rule.
The ten scores split into two groups of five. Under the stated rule, \(Q_1=46\), the median is \(51\), and \(Q_3=55\). No observation is removed in the even case.

blocks.title: Find quartiles from two equal halves
blocks.prompt:
Find the median, lower quartile, upper quartile and interquartile range of these six values:

\[12,\ 6,\ 25,\ 16,\ 10,\ 19.\]

Quartile rule: use the median of each half of the ordered data. Exclude the overall median from both halves when the number of observations is odd.
blocks.hint: Order all six values. Split them into the first three and the last three; do not insert the calculated median as a new observation.

blocks.html: For an odd count, remove only the one middle observation when forming halves, even if other observations have the same value. For an even count, do not remove the two middle observations or insert their average as a new observation.

The median describes the centre; the IQR describes central spread. A smaller IQR means that the central observations are more tightly grouped. Changing an extreme value can change the range while leaving the median and quartiles unchanged, but adding observations or changing values around the middle can alter the statistics: check again.

sections.title: Which display preserves the information I need?
sections.label: Purpose and information retained
sections.intro: Choose a representation for the question being asked. A small numerical data set can often be shown in full; a large one may need a summary. Categorical counts can be compared in a bar chart, whereas stem-and-leaf diagrams need numerical values with a meaningful order.

blocks.html:
DisplayUseful forInformation retained or lost
Ordered stem-and-leafA small or moderate numerical data setPreserves every recorded value and repetition; normally loses collection order and individual labels.
Box plotCompact comparisons of centre and spreadShows selected summary values; does not normally recover all individual observations.
HistogramThe distribution of grouped numerical dataShows class frequencies through areas; individual values within classes are lost.
Cumulative frequency graphRunning totals and estimated quantiles for grouped dataShows how many records fall below class boundaries; within-class values are not recovered.

blocks.title: Choose a display for the purpose
blocks.prompt: A teacher wants a compact comparison of the median and interquartile range of scores in two classes. Choose a suitable display. Then decide whether that display alone recovers every score, and what an ordered stem-and-leaf diagram normally loses.

options.box: Two box plots on a common score scale.
options.labels: A bar chart of pupil identifiers.

fields.label: Can the chosen display recover every individual score?

options.no: No; it shows selected summary values.
options.yes: Yes; each observation is individually preserved.
options.onlymedian: Yes, provided both medians are known.

fields.label: Information normally lost by an ordered stem-and-leaf diagram

options.order: The original order in which observations were collected.

blocks.hint: Match the representation to the comparison, then distinguish raw observations from summaries.
blocks.solution:
1. Two box plots on the same scale show the two medians and the spans between the quartiles compactly.

  2. A box plot alone does not list every individual score. Many different data sets can share the same summary values.

  3. An ordered stem-and-leaf diagram preserves the recorded values and their multiplicities, but sorting normally loses their collection order and individual labels.

blocks.html:
Give a reason tied to the task: “a stem-and-leaf diagram preserves each recorded height” or “box plots compare the medians and IQRs compactly”. A diagram of rounded measurements preserves the recorded values, not extra precision that was never measured.

When a bar chart represents counts by bar length, use a zero baseline: truncating that scale exaggerates the visual comparison.

glossary.definition: One recorded value, including each separate occurrence of a repeated value.
The property recorded for each person, item or event.
Describes a category or label, even when the label is written as a number.
Describes a numerical quantity, such as a count or measurement.
Has separate possible numerical values, as a count does.
An underlying measurement can take any value in an interval.
Leading digits and one final digit that together represent a recorded value, according to the key.
The middle observation in ordered data, or the average of the two middle observations.
Here, \(Q_1\) and \(Q_3\) are the medians of the lower and upper halves under the stated rule.
The difference \(Q_3-Q_1\), describing the spread of the central part of the data.

examples.title: Build an ordered diagram without losing an observation
examples.question:
Nine seedling heights, recorded to the nearest \(0.1\,\mathrm{cm}\), are

\[3.7,\ 2.4,\ 5.1,\ 3.0,\ 2.1,\ 3.9,\ 2.8,\ 3.2,\ 2.4.\]

Construct an ordered stem-and-leaf diagram with a key.
solution: Use the whole-number part as the stem and the tenths digit as the leaf. Thus \(2\mid4\) means \(2.4\,\mathrm{cm}\).
Place every observation on its stem. The two records of \(2.4\) need two leaves \(4\). The record \(3.0\) needs a leaf \(0\).

StemLeaves
\(2\)\(1\quad4\quad4\quad8\)
\(3\)\(0\quad2\quad7\quad9\)
\(4\)
\(5\)\(1\)

Key: \(2\mid4\) represents \(2.4\,\mathrm{cm}\).
Check the count: \(4+4+0+1=9\) leaves. The empty stem \(4\) shows that no recorded height lies from \(4.0\) to \(4.9\,\mathrm{cm}\); it is not an extra observation.

examples.title: Split a crowded stem into two labelled rows
examples.question: The test scores, in marks, are \(42,\ 44,\ 46,\ 49,\ 50,\ 52,\ 54,\ 55,\ 58,\ 63\). Construct a split stem-and-leaf diagram, using a first row for leaves \(0\) to \(4\) and a second row for leaves \(5\) to \(9\).
solution: Use tens as stems and units as leaves. Repeat each stem twice, keeping the lower leaf group before the upper group.

StemAllowed leavesLeaves
\(4\)\(0\text{ to }4\)\(2\quad4\)
\(4\)\(5\text{ to }9\)\(6\quad9\)
\(5\)\(0\text{ to }4\)\(0\quad2\quad4\)
\(5\)\(5\text{ to }9\)\(5\quad8\)
\(6\)\(0\text{ to }4\)\(3\)
\(6\)\(5\text{ to }9\)

Key: \(4\mid2\) represents \(42\) marks. Each stem has a lower and an upper leaf row.
The leaf \(4\) in the first row of stem \(5\) represents \(54\) marks. The leaf \(5\) belongs in its second row and represents \(55\) marks.
There are \(2+2+3+2+1+0=10\) leaves. The final empty row completes the stated split-stem pattern; it adds no score.

examples.title: Exclude the overall median when the count is odd
examples.question:
The ordered seedling heights, in centimetres, are \(2.1,\ 2.4,\ 2.4,\ 2.8,\ 3.0,\ 3.2,\ 3.7,\ 3.9,\ 5.1\). Find the median, quartiles, interquartile range and range.

Quartile rule: use the median of each half of the ordered data. Exclude the overall median from both halves when the number of observations is odd.
solution:
There are \(n=9\) observations. The median is the fifth value:

\[Q_2=3.0\,\mathrm{cm}.\]

Exclude that one middle observation when forming the halves:

\[\text{lower half: }2.1,\ 2.4,\ 2.4,\ 2.8;\]\[\text{upper half: }3.2,\ 3.7,\ 3.9,\ 5.1.\]
\[\mathrm{IQR}=3.8-2.4=1.4\,\mathrm{cm}.\]

\[\text{range}=5.1-2.1=3.0\,\mathrm{cm}.\]

The range uses the extremes; the IQR describes the spread of the central part of the data.

examples.title: Keep every observation when the count is even
examples.question:
The ordered test scores, in marks, are \(42,\ 44,\ 46,\ 49,\ 50,\ 52,\ 54,\ 55,\ 58,\ 63\). Find the median, quartiles and interquartile range.

Quartile rule: use the median of each half of the ordered data. Exclude the overall median from both halves when the number of observations is odd.
solution:
There are \(10\) scores, so average the fifth and sixth:

\[Q_2=\frac{50+52}{2}=51\text{ marks}.\]

Split the actual observations into equal halves:

\[\text{lower half: }42,\ 44,\ 46,\ 49,\ 50;\]\[\text{upper half: }52,\ 54,\ 55,\ 58,\ 63.\]

Each half contains five observations. Its median is its third value:

\[Q_1=46,\qquad Q_3=55.\]

\[\mathrm{IQR}=55-46=9\text{ marks}.\]

The calculated median \(51\) is not an extra score to insert into either half.

extraPractice.title: Classify what is measured, not how it is written
extraPractice.prompt: A survey records a bus route number, the number of passengers and journey duration rounded to the nearest minute. Classify the three underlying variables. A separate mass diagram has key \(2\mid6=2.6\) g; decode \(12\mid3\).

retry.feedback: The underlying duration is a measurement. Rounding its recorded value does not turn the underlying variable into a count.

extraPractice.hint: A numerical label names a category. Counts and measurements describe different kinds of quantities. Read both parts of the stem key.
extraPractice.solution:
1. The route number is a category label, so it is qualitative. The passenger count takes whole-number values, so it is discrete quantitative. Underlying duration can vary continuously; rounding the recorded duration does not change that underlying variable into a count.

  2. The key puts the leaf in the tenths place, so \(12\mid3\) represents \(12.3\) g. A stem may contain more than one digit; the leaf remains one digit.

extraPractice.title: Keep every copy while arranging the leaves
extraPractice.prompt:
The following recorded times are in seconds:

\[34,27,19,34,42,21,48,30,27,51,23.\]

Draw an ordered stem-and-leaf diagram with a key on paper. Then enter the observation count, the smallest value and the greatest value.
extraPractice.hint: Group by tens, sort the single-digit leaves, and retain both copies of each repeated time. Count leaves to check the diagram.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[19,21,23,27,27,30,34,34,42,48,51.\]
  2. StemLeaves
    1\(9\)
    2\(1\quad3\quad7\quad7\)
    3\(0\quad4\quad4\)
    4\(2\quad8\)
    5\(1\)

  3. Key: \(3\mid4\) represents \(34\) seconds. The rows contain \(1+4+3+2+1=11\) leaves. Thus \(n=11\), minimum \(19\) s and maximum \(51\) s. The repeated leaves represent distinct observations with equal recorded values.

extraPractice.title: An even data set can have odd-sized halves
extraPractice.prompt:
Find the median, both quartiles and IQR of these ten observations:

\[4,7,9,11,13,15,18,20,24,30.\]

Use medians of the lower and upper halves for quartiles; exclude the overall median when the number of observations is odd.

retry.feedback: Under the stated halves convention, the lower half has five observations; its middle value is the third one, 9.

extraPractice.hint: The overall median averages positions five and six. Each half then has five observations, so its median is one actual observation.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[\mathrm{median}=\frac{13+15}{2}=14.\]

  2. The lower half is \(4,7,9,11,13\); its middle observation is \(9\). The upper half is \(15,18,20,24,30\); its middle observation is \(20\).

  3. \[Q_1=9,\qquad Q_3=20,\qquad\mathrm{IQR}=20-9=11.\]

  4. The median is a value, not its position. Use the stated halves convention consistently; do not introduce a different software percentile rule partway through.

extraPractice.title: Read a split stem as two parts of one decade
extraPractice.prompt:
The following ordered diagram records counts. Each stem is split into a low row for leaves \(0\)–\(4\) and a high row for leaves \(5\)–\(9\).

StemLeaves
2 low\(0\quad1\quad3\quad4\)
2 high\(5\quad5\quad8\)
3 low\(0\quad2\)
3 high\(7\)

Key: a stem \(2\) with leaf \(5\) represents \(25\) items. Find the number of observations at most \(25\), the median and the range.

fields.label: Number at most the stated count

extraPractice.hint: Read both rows of a stem before moving to the next stem. “At most” includes equality and both copies of a repeated boundary value.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[20,21,23,24,25,25,28,30,32,37.\]

  2. Six observations are at most \(25\). There are ten observations altogether; the middle two are both \(25\), so their mean is \(25\).

  3. \[\mathrm{range}=37-20=17.\]

  4. The split changes the layout, not the recorded values or their total frequency.

extraPractice.title: Match a display to the information needed
extraPractice.prompt:
Choose a suitable display for each purpose. In each case explain your choice on paper.

A: Keep all \(18\) individual recorded heights visible in a compact ordered display.

B: Show the shape of a distribution of \(5000\) masses when only grouped class frequencies are available.

options.hist: Histogram with correct class widths and density scale
options.pie: Pie chart of every individual mass

extraPractice.hint: Decide whether the original records are available and whether the purpose is to preserve exact values or summarise a grouped distribution.
extraPractice.solution:
1. A: A stem-and-leaf diagram preserves each of the small set of recorded heights. A box plot or grouped histogram does not retain every individual value.

  2. B: A histogram represents the given grouped numerical distribution. Exact leaves cannot be reconstructed from frequencies alone. Later lessons explain why histogram bar area, with the correct class widths, represents frequency.

starters.title: A decimal key and twelve recorded measurements
starters.question:
Twelve component masses, recorded to the nearest \(0.1\) g, are:

\[2.1,2.3,2.3,2.8,3.0,3.4,3.6,3.9,4.0,4.5,4.8,5.2.\]

Draw an ordered stem-and-leaf diagram with a decimal key. Find the median, both quartiles, IQR and range.

Use medians of the lower and upper halves for quartiles; exclude the overall median when the number of observations is odd.
starters.hint: There are six values in each half. Average the middle pair of each half and use the key to restore the mass scale.
starters.solution:
1. StemLeaves
    2\(1\quad3\quad3\quad8\)
    3\(0\quad4\quad6\quad9\)
    4\(0\quad5\quad8\)
    5\(2\)

  2. Key: \(3\mid4\) represents \(3.4\) g. The diagram preserves all twelve recorded values, including the two masses recorded as \(2.3\) g.

  3. \[\mathrm{median}=\frac{3.4+3.6}{2}=3.5\ \text{g}.\]
  4. \[Q_1=\frac{2.3+2.8}{2}=2.55\ \text{g},\qquad Q_3=\frac{4.0+4.5}{2}=4.25\ \text{g}.\]
  5. \[\mathrm{IQR}=4.25-2.55=1.7\ \text{g},\qquad\mathrm{range}=5.2-2.1=3.1\ \text{g}.\]

  6. A quartile may lie between recorded values. These summaries are exact calculations for the recorded data; recording to the nearest tenth does not reveal the unrounded original masses.
starters.marking:
• 2 marks: preserve every observation in the correct ordered stem and leaf rows.
  • 1 mark: supply a correct decimal key with grams.
  • 1 mark: obtain the overall median from the middle two values.
  • 1 mark: obtain the lower-half median.
  • 1 mark: obtain the upper-half median.
  • 1 mark: calculate and label the IQR.
  • 1 mark: calculate and label the range.

starters.title: One extreme record changes while its rank stays last
starters.question:
The ordered counts from fifteen days are:

\[8,10,10,12,14,15,18,20,23,24,25,28,31,33,35.\]

The final record is corrected from \(35\) to \(80\). Find the median, IQR and range of the corrected data. Explain on paper why these summaries do not all change.

Use medians of the lower and upper halves for quartiles; exclude the overall median when the number of observations is odd.
starters.hint: The corrected record remains the greatest value. Identify the positions used for the median and both half medians before recomputing.
starters.solution:
1. There are still fifteen observations. The median is position eight, so it stays \(20\). Exclude that observation before splitting.

  2. The lower seven observations have middle value \(12\), and the upper seven have middle value \(28\). Neither selected observation was changed.

  3. \[Q_1=12,\qquad Q_3=28,\qquad\mathrm{IQR}=16.\]
  4. \[\mathrm{range}=80-8=72.\]

  5. The old range was \(35-8=27\). The range changes because it uses the maximum. The median and quartiles remain unchanged in this particular correction because their selected positions and values are unchanged. Adding or removing records could change those positions, so this is not a rule that every change to extreme data leaves the IQR fixed.
starters.marking:
• 1 mark: identify the unchanged count and median position.
  • 1 mark: obtain the median.
  • 1 mark: identify both half medians using the stated convention.
  • 1 mark: obtain the IQR.
  • 1 mark: obtain the new range.
  • 1 mark: explain the different effects using the unchanged selected ranks and changed maximum.

revision.body:
Read the variable and key, preserve every record, then count ordered positions.

Classify the underlying variable

Qualitative: categories, including numerical identifiers. Discrete quantitative: separated numerical possibilities, such as a count. Continuous quantitative: measurements such as mass or time. A continuous measurement remains continuous when its recorded value is rounded.

Construct and decode a stem-and-leaf diagram

Choose a place-value scale. Order the stems and the single-digit leaves. Keep repetitions and empty intermediate stems; count all leaves to check the total. A stem can contain several digits.

Give a key with units: \(2\mid4=2.4\) cm. For split stems use a low row with leaves \(0\)–\(4\) and a high row with leaves \(5\)–\(9\). Splitting changes layout, not the observations.

Use ordered positions and the stated quartile convention

For odd \(n\), the median is observation \(\frac{n+1}{2}\). For even \(n\), average observations \(\frac{n}{2}\) and \(\frac{n}{2}+1\).

Here \(Q_1\) and \(Q_3\) are the medians of the lower and upper halves. Exclude the overall median when \(n\) is odd; split even data into two equal halves. Follow a different convention if a question explicitly supplies one.

\[\mathrm{IQR}=Q_3-Q_1,\qquad\mathrm{range}=\mathrm{maximum}-\mathrm{minimum}.\]

These are differences of values, not of positions; retain the original units.

Choose a display by its purpose

A stem-and-leaf display preserves each recorded value and is useful for a small data set. Grouped displays summarise larger data sets but lose individual values. A box plot highlights selected summaries; a histogram shows a grouped numerical distribution. A key, readable scale and honest labelling are essential. Recorded rounded data cannot recover the original unrounded measurements.
revision.checks:
• Variable distinguished from its label and recording accuracy?
  • Key, units, ordered leaves and repeated values included?
  • All observations counted, including both split-stem rows?
  • Quartile halves formed consistently before calculating IQR?
revision.examTip: Quartile halves formed consistently before calculating IQR?

sections.title: How do I read the two sides correctly?
sections.label: Mirrored leaves and separate counts
sections.intro: A back-to-back diagram places two samples on opposite sides of shared stems. Give both sample names and a key that explains each side in the same units. The rows share a scale, but the samples keep their own observations and counts.

blocks.html:
On the right, ordered leaves increase from left to right. On the left, they decrease from left to right: the smallest leaf is nearest the stem. To decode a left row in increasing order, start at the stem and read outwards.

Count every leaf on each side independently, including repetitions and zero leaves. Keep empty stems where needed. If stems are split, use the same labelled leaf groups on both sides.
Sample A has \(8\) observations and B has \(9\). Their shared stems do not make the counts equal. The key decodes a leaf on either side into a complete time.

blocks.title: Decode each side separately
blocks.prompt:
The two samples contain recorded times.

A leavesStemB leaves
\(8\quad4\)\(1\)\(2\quad9\)
\(6\quad2\quad0\)\(2\)\(1\quad1\quad5\quad8\)

Key: left leaf \(4\), stem \(1\), right leaf \(2\) mean \(14\,\mathrm{s}\) in A and \(12\,\mathrm{s}\) in B. Find each sample size, the least A time, and the number of B times equal to \(21\,\mathrm{s}\).

fields.label: Number of B observations at the stated time

blocks.hint: On the left, read from the stem outwards within each row. Count leaves independently on the two sides.
blocks.solution:
1. \[A:\quad14,\ 18,\ 20,\ 22,\ 26;\qquad n_A=5.\]
  2. \[B:\quad12,\ 19,\ 21,\ 21,\ 25,\ 28;\qquad n_B=6.\]

  3. The least A time is \(14\,\mathrm{s}\). The two leaves \(1\) beside stem \(2\) in B represent two separate records of \(21\,\mathrm{s}\).

blocks.html: Do not read the whole left side from left to right as if it were an increasing list. Decode by stem first, then order that sample’s values before selecting positions.

sections.title: How do I compare two samples fairly?
sections.label: Centre, spread and proportions
sections.intro: Use each sample’s own count to find its median and quartiles. For an even count, the median averages the two middle observations; for an odd count, it is the single middle observation.

blocks.html:
Quartile convention: take the medians of the lower and upper halves, excluding the overall median from both halves when the count is odd.

Write one comparison of centre using the medians, and one of spread using the IQRs. Give the values, units and what they mean in context. A smaller IQR means the central observations are more tightly grouped.

blocks.title: Compare typical time, spread and proportions
blocks.prompt:
Two task-time samples have these summaries. All times are in seconds.

SampleCountMedianIQRCount at most \(22\) seconds
A\(6\)\(18\)\(5\)\(4\)
B\(9\)\(21\)\(4\)\(5\)

Which sample has the lower typical completion time? Which has less central spread? Find the proportion at most \(22\) seconds in each sample.
blocks.hint: Use the median for typical time, IQR for central spread, and each sample’s own count for its proportion.
blocks.solution:
1. A has the lower median, \(18\) rather than \(21\) seconds, so its recorded completion times are typically shorter.

  2. B has the smaller IQR, \(4\) rather than \(5\) seconds, so its central times are more tightly grouped.

  3. \[p_A=\frac{4}{6}=\frac{2}{3},\qquad p_B=\frac{5}{9}.\]

  4. Although B has more qualifying records, A has the larger proportion: \(\frac{2}{3}>\frac{5}{9}\).

blocks.html:
For unequal sample sizes, compare proportions rather than raw counts when describing how often a condition is met:

\[\text{proportion}=\frac{\text{qualifying observations}}{\text{sample size}}.\]

Read a threshold carefully: “below” excludes equality, while “at most” includes it. Keep conclusions about the observed samples; a lower median does not mean every individual value is lower.

sections.title: How can a mean recover a missing record?
sections.label: Totals and changed sample sizes
sections.intro:
The mean is the total divided by the number of observations. If the mean is given exactly, reverse this calculation:

\[\overline{x}=\frac{T}{n},\qquad T=n\overline{x}.\]

blocks.html: For one missing record, subtract the sum of the known records from the required total. Then insert the result and check the mean. If a record is added or removed, update both the total and the count before finding a new mean.

blocks.title: Recover a missing record, then update the count
blocks.prompt: Six numerical records are \(8,11,13,16,17,x\), with mean \(14\). Find \(x\). The record \(8\) is then removed; find the mean of the five remaining records.
blocks.hint: The original total is six times the mean. Removing one record changes both the total and the number of records.

blocks.html: Correcting an existing record keeps the count unchanged: subtract the wrong value and add its replacement to the total. To recalculate a median or quartile, put the updated records back in order and use the updated count. One mean condition for two unknown records usually fixes only their sum.

sections.title: How do I recover missing leaves without guessing?
sections.label: Digit limits, positions and all answers
sections.intro: A missing leaf is an integer digit from \(0\) to \(9\). Its place value comes from the key: on a tens stem \(2\), leaf \(a\) represents \(20+a\), not \(a\). The neighbouring leaves add order restrictions, with the direction reversed on the left side.

blocks.html:
1. Decode the complete ordered observations.
  2. Write the digit and row-order restrictions.
  3. Identify the positions used by the supplied statistic.
  4. Form an equation and keep every permitted digit choice.
  5. Insert each answer into the original diagram and check every condition.
The left row forces \(2\le h\le4\). All three digits give median \(25.5\), but only \(h=4\) gives IQR \(9\).

blocks.title: Use the mirrored order before solving for a leaf
blocks.prompt:
The left side of an ordered diagram is shown below. Each row is printed from left to right.

Left leavesStem
\(7\quad2\)\(1\)
\(8\quad b\quad2\)\(2\)
\(4\)\(3\)

A left leaf \(2\) beside stem \(1\) means \(12\,\mathrm{s}\). Give every digit \(b\) permitted by the row order alone. Then find \(b\) if the median is \(24.5\,\mathrm{s}\).

fields.label: Digit fixed by the stated median

blocks.hint: Decode the ordered values as \(12,17,22,20+b,28,34\). The median uses the third and fourth observations.
blocks.solution:
1. The left row decreases towards the stem, so \(8\ge b\ge2\). The allowed integer digits are \(2,3,4,5,6,7,8\).

  2. \[\frac{22+(20+b)}{2}=24.5\Longrightarrow42+b=49\Longrightarrow b=7.\]

  3. The recovered list is \(12,17,22,27,28,34\). Its row order is valid and its median is \(24.5\,\mathrm{s}\).

blocks.html: A summary may not determine a missing leaf uniquely. If all remaining digits or pairs satisfy the conditions, report all of them. Do not assume leaves are distinct, and do not impose an order on labelled records unless the diagram or question supplies one.

sections.title: How can I combine or reverse numerical summaries?
sections.label: Application after mean and variance
sections.intro:
Later-chapter application: use this section after studying means, variance and standard deviation. It connects those summaries to the records preserved in stem diagrams; the core diagram methods above do not depend on it.

The descriptive variance measures squared spread around the mean. Here its divisor is the number of observations \(n\), and the standard deviation \(\sigma\) is its square root:

\[\sigma^2=\frac{\sum x^2}{n}-\overline{x}^{\,2}.\]

blocks.html:
Recover two additive totals for each nonempty sample:

\[T=\sum x=n\overline{x},\qquad U=\sum x^2=n\bigl(\sigma^2+\overline{x}^{\,2}\bigr).\]

For separate groups measuring the same variable in the same units, add their counts, totals and totals of squares. Then

\[\overline{x}_{\mathrm{all}}=\frac{T_A+T_B}{n_A+n_B},\qquad\sigma^2_{\mathrm{all}}=\frac{U_A+U_B}{n_A+n_B}-\overline{x}_{\mathrm{all}}^{\,2}.\]

With missing records, subtract the known contributions from \(T\) and \(U\). For two unknowns, this gives equations for their sum and their sum of squares. Solve both equations and check every labelled pair against the original information.

blocks.title: Application: recover two labelled observations from summaries
blocks.prompt: Application after mean and variance: five data values are \(4,7,9,x,y\). Their mean is \(8\), and their descriptive variance, using divisor \(5\), is \(\frac{28}{5}\). Find every ordered pair \((x,y)\). The letters label different records; no order between their values is assumed.
blocks.hint: Recover the total and the total of squares. They give equations for \(x+y\) and \(x^2+y^2\).
blocks.solution:
1. \[\sum x=5(8)=40\Longrightarrow x+y=40-(4+7+9)=20.\]
  2. \[\sum x^2=5\left(\frac{28}{5}+8^2\right)=348.\]\[x^2+y^2=348-(4^2+7^2+9^2)=202.\]

  3. Substitute \(y=20-x\):

    \[x^2+(20-x)^2=202\Longrightarrow x^2-20x+99=0.\]
  4. \[(x-9)(x-11)=0\Longrightarrow(x,y)=(9,11)\text{ or }(11,9).\]

  5. Both pairs give the required total and total of squares. Since the labels are not ordered by value, retain both.

blocks.html: The total of squares \(\sum x^2\) is not the square of the total \((\sum x)^2\). If a question gives standard deviation, square it before recovering \(U\). Variance has squared data units; standard deviation has the original units. These formulas use the stated descriptive divisor \(n\).

glossary.definition: The particular group of observations being described or compared.
The number \(n\) of observations, counting every repeated value separately.
An explanation of how a leaf on each side of the shared stems represents a complete value, including its units.
The middle of the ordered observations, or the average of the two middle observations for an even count.
The central spread \(Q_3-Q_1\), using the stated quartile convention.
The number of qualifying observations divided by that sample’s total count.
Separate observations whose labels do not automatically put their values in increasing order.
The total \(\sum x^2\), formed by squaring each value before adding; it differs from \((\sum x)^2\).
The average squared distance from the data mean, using divisor \(n\). Standard deviation is its square root.

examples.title: Use shared stems while keeping two separate samples
examples.question:
Recorded task times, in seconds, are

A: \(21,\ 22,\ 24,\ 24,\ 27,\ 31,\ 33,\ 36\).

B: \(19,\ 23,\ 26,\ 29,\ 29,\ 32,\ 35,\ 37,\ 41\).

Construct a back-to-back stem-and-leaf diagram with A on the left, and state each sample size.
solution: Use tens as the shared stems and units as leaves. On the left, print the larger leaves farther from the stem; on the right, print them farther to the right.

Sample A leavesStemSample B leaves
\(1\)\(9\)
\(7\quad4\quad4\quad2\quad1\)\(2\)\(3\quad6\quad9\quad9\)
\(6\quad3\quad1\)\(3\)\(2\quad5\quad7\)
\(4\)\(1\)

Two-sided key: left leaf \(4\), stem \(2\), right leaf \(3\) represent \(24\,\mathrm{s}\) in A and \(23\,\mathrm{s}\) in B.
In A, stem \(2\) is read from the stem outwards as \(21,22,24,24,27\). In B, that row reads \(23,26,29,29\).

\[n_A=5+3=8,\qquad n_B=1+4+3+1=9.\]

Repeated leaves are separate observations. Empty rows on one side do not change the count on the other.

examples.title: Compare the centre and spread in context
examples.question:
For the task times

A: \(21,\ 22,\ 24,\ 24,\ 27,\ 31,\ 33,\ 36\); B: \(19,\ 23,\ 26,\ 29,\ 29,\ 32,\ 35,\ 37,\ 41\),

calculate the medians and IQRs, compare the samples in context, and compare the proportions below \(30\,\mathrm{s}\).

Quartile rule: use the median of each half of the ordered data, excluding the overall median from both halves when the count is odd.
solution:
A has eight observations:

\[Q_{2,A}=\frac{24+27}{2}=25.5,\quad Q_{1,A}=\frac{22+24}{2}=23,\quad Q_{3,A}=\frac{31+33}{2}=32.\]\[\mathrm{IQR}_A=32-23=9\,\mathrm{s}.\]

B has nine observations. Exclude the fifth value when forming its halves:

\[Q_{2,B}=29,\quad Q_{1,B}=\frac{23+26}{2}=24.5,\quad Q_{3,B}=\frac{35+37}{2}=36.\]\[\mathrm{IQR}_B=36-24.5=11.5\,\mathrm{s}.\]

A has the lower median, \(25.5\) rather than \(29\) seconds, so completion is typically faster in sample A. Its smaller IQR, \(9\) rather than \(11.5\) seconds, shows less variation among the central observations.

Both samples have five observations below \(30\,\mathrm{s}\), but

\[\frac{5}{8}>\frac{5}{9}.\]

The proportion is greater in A because its total count is smaller.
These are statements about the recorded samples. They do not say every A time is shorter than every B time, or establish why the samples differ.

examples.title: Use a mean to recover a total
examples.question: Five scores are \(9,12,16,18,x\), with mean \(15\). Find \(x\). A sixth score of \(30\) is then added; find the new mean.
solution: \[\text{total of five scores}=5(15)=75.\]

Check: \(9+12+16+18+20=75\). After adding the new score, both the total and the count change:

\[\text{new total}=75+30=105,\qquad\text{new count}=6.\]

\[\text{new mean}=\frac{105}{6}=17.5.\]

The new score exceeds the old mean, so an increased mean is sensible.

examples.title: A quartile can identify a leaf that the median cannot
examples.question:
Sample A is the left side of an ordered time diagram. Its rows are

A leaves, printed left to rightStem
\(7\quad4\quad h\quad2\quad1\)\(2\)
\(6\quad3\quad1\)\(3\)

A left leaf \(4\) beside stem \(2\) means \(24\,\mathrm{s}\). Find \(h\) if the IQR is \(9\,\mathrm{s}\), and explain why a median of \(25.5\,\mathrm{s}\) alone would not determine it.

Quartile rule: use the median of each half of the ordered data, excluding the overall median from both halves when the count is odd.
solution:
The row order requires \(2\le h\le4\), so initially

\[h\in\{2,3,4\}.\]

The ordered values are \(21,22,20+h,24,27,31,33,36\).

\[Q_2=\frac{24+27}{2}=25.5\,\mathrm{s}.\]

These two positions do not involve \(h\), so all three candidate digits give the same median.
\[\mathrm{IQR}=32-\left(21+\frac{h}{2}\right)=11-\frac{h}{2}.\]\[11-\frac{h}{2}=9\Longrightarrow h=4.\]
This is an allowed digit, preserves the mirrored row order, and gives \(Q_1=23\), \(Q_3=32\) and IQR \(9\) seconds.

examples.title: List every digit pair that satisfies the information
examples.question:
An ordered ordinary stem-and-leaf diagram is

StemLeaves
\(1\)\(1\quad5\)
\(2\)\(2\quad a\quad b\quad9\)
\(3\)\(1\quad6\)

The key is \(2\mid2=22\). The median is \(24\). Find all possible digit pairs \((a,b)\).
solution:
The ordered row requires integer digits satisfying

\[2\le a\le b\le9.\]

There are eight observations. The fourth and fifth values are \(20+a\) and \(20+b\), so

\[\frac{(20+a)+(20+b)}{2}=24\Longrightarrow a+b=8.\]
Since \(a\le b=8-a\), we have \(a\le4\). Combining this with \(a\ge2\) gives only \(a=2,3,4\).
Every pair respects the digit and row restrictions and gives median \(24\). Repeated leaves are allowed, so \((4,4)\) is valid. The given information does not select one unique pair.

examples.title: Application: combine totals instead of averaging summaries
examples.question: Application after mean and standard deviation: one group of four plant heights has mean \(12\,\mathrm{cm}\) and standard deviation \(3\,\mathrm{cm}\). A different group of six has mean \(17\,\mathrm{cm}\) and standard deviation \(4\,\mathrm{cm}\). Each descriptive variance uses its own group count as divisor. Find the mean, variance and standard deviation of all ten heights.
solution:
Recover each total and total of squares:

\[T_A=4(12)=48,\qquad U_A=4(3^2+12^2)=612;\]\[T_B=6(17)=102,\qquad U_B=6(4^2+17^2)=1830.\]
\[\overline{x}=\frac{150}{10}=15\,\mathrm{cm}.\]

The groups have different sizes, so the unweighted mean of their two means would be wrong. Their standard deviations cannot simply be averaged: differences between the group means also contribute to the combined spread.

extraPractice.title: Compare typical time and central spread separately
extraPractice.prompt:
The diagram records task times in seconds for two groups.

AStemB
\(8\quad 7\quad 4\quad 2\)1\(1\quad 5\quad 6\quad 9\)
\(8\quad 5\quad 2\)2\(0\quad 4\quad 7\)

Key: \(4\mid1\mid5\) means \(14\) s for A and \(15\) s for B. Find each median and IQR, then select the supported comparison.

Use the median of each half for quartiles, excluding the overall middle observation when the count is odd.

options.tradeoff: A has a lower median time, but a larger IQR.
options.all: Every A observation is faster than every B observation.
options.same: Both samples have the same centre and spread.

extraPractice.hint: Read each left row from the stem outwards when listing values in ascending order. Calculate the summaries for each sample separately.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[A:12,14,17,18,22,25,28;\qquad B:11,15,16,19,20,24,27.\]

  2. Each sample contains seven times, so its median is the fourth observation. Thus the medians are \(18\) s and \(19\) s.

  3. \[Q_{1,A}=14,\quad Q_{3,A}=25,\quad\mathrm{IQR}_A=11\ \text{s};\]
  4. \[Q_{1,B}=15,\quad Q_{3,B}=24,\quad\mathrm{IQR}_B=9\ \text{s}.\]

  5. Group A was typically faster by the median, but its central times were less consistent because its IQR was larger. The distributions overlap; a lower median does not say that every individual A time was lower.

extraPractice.title: Unequal sample sizes require proportions
extraPractice.prompt:
Recorded completion times, in seconds, are:

\[A:10,12,14,18,20;\]\[B:9,11,13,15,16,17,19,21,23,25.\]

Find the fraction of each sample completing in at most \(18\) seconds. Which sample had the greater observed fraction meeting this target?
extraPractice.hint: “At most” includes equality. Divide each successful count by its own sample size.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[p_A=\frac{4}{5},\qquad p_B=\frac{6}{10}=\frac{3}{5}.\]

  2. A has the greater observed fraction: \(80\%\) compared with \(60\%\). B has more successful observations in absolute number, but its sample is twice as large.

  3. This compares the recorded samples. These counts alone do not prove that one method will perform better in every future setting.

extraPractice.title: A missing record changes both the total and the count
extraPractice.prompt: Five recorded values are \(12,15,18,20,25\). One omitted value is restored, making the mean of all six values \(18\). Find the restored value and the median of the corrected data.

retry.feedback: The restored data contain six values, not five. Their total is six times the new mean.

extraPractice.hint: The target total is six times the new mean. Insert the restored value in order before finding the middle pair.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[\text{Known total}=12+15+18+20+25=90.\]
  2. \[\text{New total}=6\times18=108,\qquad x=108-90=18.\]
  3. \[12,15,18,18,20,25\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\mathrm{median}=\frac{18+18}{2}=18.\]

  4. The repeated value is a separate observation. Dividing by the old count of five would not describe the corrected sample.

extraPractice.title: Summary values need not determine one missing leaf
extraPractice.prompt:
An ordered stem-and-leaf diagram has stems \(1,2,3\), with right-hand leaf rows \((1,5,8)\), \((a,4,7)\), and \((1,6,9)\). The key is \(2\mid4=24\). The median is \(24\) and the IQR is \(17\). Find every possible single-digit value of \(a\), allowing repeated leaves.

Use the median of each half for quartiles, excluding the overall middle observation when the count is odd.
extraPractice.hint: First impose the digit and row-order restrictions. Then identify the positions used in the given median and IQR: do they actually involve the missing leaf?
extraPractice.solution:
1. The ordered row requires \(0\le a\le4\), with \(a\) an integer. The ordered observations are

    \[11,15,18,20+a,24,27,31,36,39.\]

  2. The median is the fifth observation, \(24\), for every allowed digit. Excluding that observation, the half medians are

    \[Q_1=\frac{15+18}{2}=\frac{33}{2},\qquad Q_3=\frac{31+36}{2}=\frac{67}{2}.\]
  3. \[\mathrm{IQR}=\frac{67}{2}-\frac{33}{2}=17.\]

  4. Neither summary selects the fourth observation. Every digit \(0,1,2,3,4\) therefore satisfies all conditions. The data do not determine a unique missing value.

extraPractice.title: Mixed application: pool totals, not standard deviations
extraPractice.prompt: Mixed application — mean and descriptive variance. One group of four daily counts has mean \(8\) and standard deviation \(\sqrt{5}\). A second group of six counts has mean \(13\) and standard deviation \(2\). Both standard deviations use the descriptive divisor \(n\). Find the combined mean and variance.
extraPractice.hint: Recover the sum and sum of squares for each group. Add those totals and the counts, then calculate the combined summaries.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[T_1=4(8)=32,\quad T_2=6(13)=78,\quad N=10,\quad\bar{x}=\frac{110}{10}=11.\]
  2. \[U_1=4\bigl((\sqrt{5})^2+8^2\bigr)=276,\qquad U_2=6(2^2+13^2)=1038.\]
  3. \[U=1314,\qquad\sigma^2=\frac{1314}{10}-11^2=\frac{52}{5}.\]

  4. The means have different sample weights. The combined variance also includes the separation between the two group means; averaging the two standard deviations would not account for that.

starters.title: Recover a left-hand leaf before comparing two samples
starters.question:
The diagram records completion times in minutes. The missing leaf \(a\) is a single digit, and each row is ordered outwards from the stem.

AStemB
\(8\quad 6\quad 3\)1\(4\quad 7\)
\(9\quad 7\quad 4\quad a\)2\(0\quad 3\quad 5\quad 8\)
\(2\)3\(1\)

Key: \(4\mid2\mid5\) means \(24\) min for A and \(25\) min for B. The median of A is \(23\) min. Find \(a\), both IQRs and both ranges. Compare the samples in context on paper.

Use the median of each half for quartiles, excluding the overall middle observation when the count is odd.
starters.hint: A has eight records and B has seven. On the left-hand stem two, the leaf nearest the stem is \(a\), so row order requires \(a\le4\).
starters.solution:
1. \[A:13,16,18,20+a,24,27,29,32,\qquad0\le a\le4.\]
  2. \[\frac{20+a+24}{2}=23\Longrightarrow a=2.\]

  3. The accepted digit preserves row order. For A, the two four-value halves give

    \[Q_{1,A}=\frac{16+18}{2}=17,\quad Q_{3,A}=\frac{27+29}{2}=28,\quad\mathrm{IQR}_A=11\ \text{min}.\]
  4. \[B:14,17,20,23,25,28,31.\]

  5. B has median \(23\) min, lower quartile \(17\) min and upper quartile \(28\) min, so its IQR is also \(11\) min.

  6. \[\mathrm{range}_A=32-13=19\ \text{min},\qquad\mathrm{range}_B=31-14=17\ \text{min}.\]

  7. The samples have the same median completion time and the same central spread by IQR. A has a wider overall range. Equal median and IQR do not mean that the distributions or individual times are identical.
starters.marking:
• 1 mark: read the left-hand order and separate sample counts correctly.
  • 1 mark: form the correct median equation for A.
  • 1 mark: obtain and check the permitted leaf.
  • 1 mark: obtain both quartiles and IQR for A.
  • 1 mark: obtain the median and IQR for B under the stated convention.
  • 1 mark: obtain both ranges.
  • 1 mark: compare median and IQR with units and context.
  • 1 mark: distinguish equal central summaries from the different overall ranges.

starters.title: Mixed application: two missing labelled observations
starters.question: Mixed application — mean and descriptive variance. Six daily counts are \(6,8,10,12,x,y\), where \(x\) is Monday’s count and \(y\) is Tuesday’s count. The mean is \(10\), and the descriptive variance with divisor six is \(\frac{20}{3}\). Find every possible ordered pair \((x,y)\). No order relation between the two labelled counts is given.
starters.hint: Recover the total and sum of squares, then obtain the sum and product of the missing counts. Labels distinguish the two assignments.
starters.solution:
1. \[T=6(10)=60\Longrightarrow x+y=60-(6+8+10+12)=24.\]
  2. \[U=6\left(\frac{20}{3}+10^2\right)=640\Longrightarrow x^2+y^2=640-344=296.\]
  3. \[(x+y)^2=x^2+y^2+2xy\Longrightarrow xy=\frac{24^2-296}{2}=140.\]
  4. \[z^2-24z+140=(z-10)(z-14)=0.\]

  5. The missing values are \(10\) and \(14\), but either can belong to Monday. Therefore the complete answer is \((10,14)\) and \((14,10)\).

  6. Both assignments are nonnegative integer counts and restore the given total and sum of squares. Their common variance is \(\frac{640}{6}-100=\frac{20}{3}\). No extra restriction selects one labelled assignment.
starters.marking:
• 1 mark: reconstruct the total and obtain the missing-value sum.
  • 1 mark: reconstruct the full sum of squares.
  • 1 mark: subtract the known squared observations.
  • 1 mark: obtain the product or an equivalent quadratic.
  • 1 mark: solve for the two missing values.
  • 1 mark: retain both labelled assignments.
  • 1 mark: check count feasibility and both original summaries.

revision.body:
Keep each sample separate, compare centre and spread, then test every permitted missing value.

Read both sides and compare in context

Use shared stems and a two-sided unit key. Leaves increase away from each stem; left rows descend left to right. Count each sample separately.

Compare medians for typical values and IQRs for central spread. Name both samples, values, units and context. With unequal sample sizes, compare proportions. Similar summaries need not mean identical data.

Use the correct total and updated count

\[T=n\bar{x},\qquad x_{\rm missing}=T_{\rm complete}-T_{\rm known}.\]

Restoring or adding a record changes the count. Replacing a record keeps the count and changes the total by new value minus old value. Reorder the completed data before finding the median or quartiles.

Constrain missing leaves before solving

A leaf is an integer from \(0\) to \(9\). Impose row order, using equality when repeats are permitted. Locate the actual median and quartile positions for that sample size; only then form equations.

Use medians of halves; exclude the overall middle observation for odd counts. Check all digit, order and summary conditions. Retain every valid candidate and distinct labelled assignment.

Mixed application: combine summary totals

For each group, with descriptive variance \(\sigma_i^2\),

\[T_i=n_i\bar{x}_i,\qquad U_i=n_i(\sigma_i^2+\bar{x}_i^2).\]

Add the counts, totals and sums of squares:

\[N=\sum n_i,\quad\bar{x}=\frac{\sum T_i}{N},\quad\sigma^2=\frac{\sum U_i}{N}-\bar{x}^{\,2}.\]

Square a supplied standard deviation first. Do not average standard deviations or ignore the different group means. This block uses the mean and variance methods developed in the next two chapters.
revision.checks:
• Both sides decoded with the correct key and counts?
  • Centre and spread compared with numbers and context?
  • Updated total, count, ranks and repeated observations correct?
  • All permissible digits or labelled assignments checked?

orig_9709_s1_rep_histograms.description: Read the class boundaries and both scales before using a histogram. Recover frequencies from bar areas, then use midpoint models to estimate the centre and spread without confusing grouped data with the original records.

sections.title: Which boundaries define each class?
sections.label: Recorded limits and continuous intervals
sections.intro: A grouped table records how many observations fall in each interval. Write continuous classes without overlap, for example \(4\le h<8\) followed by \(8\le h<16\). A height of exactly \(8\) enters the second class.

blocks.html:
If measurements were rounded to the nearest stated precision, the boundary is half that precision beyond the recorded endpoint label. Use the stated rule for exact halfway values. Then

\[w=\text{upper boundary}-\text{lower boundary}.\]

If continuous boundaries are already supplied, use them directly.

blocks.title: Use the stated measurement precision
blocks.prompt:
Lengths are rounded to the nearest \(0.1\,\mathrm{mm}\). One class contains recorded values from \(12.0\) through \(12.9\,\mathrm{mm}\), inclusive. At an exact halfway value, round upwards. Find the continuous lower boundary, upper boundary and class width.

A separate table already defines a continuous class as \(6\le x<10\). Should its boundaries receive another half-unit adjustment?

fields.label: Adjustment for the separately stated continuous interval

options.half: Subtract and add half a unit.
options.tenth: Subtract and add one tenth of a unit.

blocks.hint: Half the rounding precision is \(0.05\,\mathrm{mm}\). Distinguish recorded class limits from boundaries already stated for the continuous variable.
blocks.solution:
1. \[12.0-0.05=11.95,\qquad12.9+0.05=12.95.\]

  2. The first class is \(11.95\le x<12.95\), in millimetres, with width

    \[12.95-11.95=1\,\mathrm{mm}.\]

  3. The separate interval \(6\le x<10\) already states its boundaries. No adjustment is required.

blocks.html: A gap between recorded labels does not by itself justify changing boundaries. Check whether the values were rounded, truncated or defined as discrete counts. For positive measurements truncated to whole units, recorded values \(10\) through \(14\) correspond to \(10\le x<15\). A genuine interval containing no observations has zero frequency; do not fill it with invented data.

sections.title: Why does a histogram use frequency density?
sections.label: Frequency is represented by area
sections.intro: A histogram represents grouped numerical data on a continuous horizontal scale. Its bars use the actual class widths. Adjacent class intervals touch, and a zero-frequency class has zero bar height.

blocks.html:
\[d=\frac{f}{w},\qquad f=wd.\]

Frequency density \(d\) is the number of observations per unit of the measured variable. With density on the vertical axis, width times height gives frequency. This makes unequal-width classes comparable.
The tallest bar has density \(3\) and frequency \(12\). The wider final bar has density \(2\) but frequency \(16\).

blocks.title: Separate the tallest bars from the largest frequency
blocks.prompt:
Lengths \(x\), in centimetres, are grouped below. Classes are numbered in increasing order.

ClassIntervalFrequency
\(1\)\(0\le x<2\)\(6\)
\(2\)\(2\le x<5\)\(9\)
\(3\)\(5\le x<10\)\(10\)

Find the three frequency densities, in observations per centimetre. Give every class number tied for the greatest density, then the class number with the greatest frequency.

fields.label: All class numbers with greatest density

blocks.hint: Divide each frequency by its own class width. Height and area answer different questions.
blocks.solution:
1. \[w_1=2,\quad w_2=3,\quad w_3=5.\]
  2. \[d_1=\frac{6}{2}=3,\quad d_2=\frac{9}{3}=3,\quad d_3=\frac{10}{5}=2.\]

  3. Classes \(1\) and \(2\) tie for greatest density. Class \(3\) contains the most observations, since its frequency is \(10\).

blocks.html: Label the measured variable and units on the horizontal axis, and frequency density on the vertical axis. Use a consistent numerical scale on each axis and draw bar heights from zero, because area encodes frequency. Calculate the width of every class before plotting it.

sections.title: What if the diagram uses a different scale?
sections.label: Paper lengths and proportional areas
sections.intro: A centimetre on paper need not represent one data unit or one density unit. Read the horizontal scale to recover a class width, and the vertical scale to recover its density. If the scale is unknown, calibrate it using a bar with a known frequency.

blocks.html:
All bars on one histogram share the same area-to-frequency scale. If a plotted height is \(H=kd\), where the common multiplier \(k>0\), then

\[f=w\frac{H}{k}.\]

For physical areas measured on paper, both drawing scales matter. Compare with a known bar or convert both dimensions before calculating frequency.

blocks.title: Calibrate a histogram drawn on paper
blocks.prompt:
A histogram uses \(1\,\mathrm{cm}\) on paper for \(2\,\mathrm{cm}\) of measured length. A class of data width \(6\,\mathrm{cm}\) has frequency \(30\), and its bar is \(2.5\,\mathrm{cm}\) tall on paper. Find how many frequency-density units one vertical centimetre represents.

On the same diagram, another class has data width \(10\,\mathrm{cm}\) and paper height \(1.5\,\mathrm{cm}\). Find its frequency.

fields.label: Density units per vertical centimetre on paper

blocks.hint: First calculate the known class’s density. Divide it by its measured paper height to calibrate the vertical scale.
blocks.solution:
1. \[d=\frac{30}{6}=5,\qquad\text{vertical scale}=\frac{5}{2.5}=2.\]

  2. The second bar represents density \(1.5(2)=3\), so

    \[f=10(3)=30.\]

  3. As a paper-area check, the first bar has area \(3(2.5)=7.5\,\mathrm{cm}^2\), representing \(30\) observations. The second has area \(5(1.5)=7.5\,\mathrm{cm}^2\), so it has the same frequency.

blocks.html: Do not multiply a class width in data units by a ruler height in centimetres without converting the height. “Bar area equals frequency” uses the stated coordinate scales; paper square centimetres may represent several observations.

sections.title: How can grouped data estimate the mean and spread?
sections.label: Midpoints, variance and standard deviation
sections.intro:
A class frequency does not reveal the original values within that class. To estimate summaries, use its midpoint \(m\) as a representative value:

\[m=\frac{\text{lower boundary}+\text{upper boundary}}{2},\qquad N=\sum f.\]

The symbol \(\sum\) means add the entries in the column. Each midpoint represents \(f\) observations, so frequencies supply the weights.

blocks.html:
Variance measures spread by averaging squared distances from the mean. For the actual \(N\) records, the descriptive formula is

\[\sigma^2=\frac{\sum(x_i-\bar{x})^2}{N}=\frac{\sum x_i^2}{N}-\bar{x}^{\,2}.\]

The standard deviation is its square root. Here we describe the given data using divisor \(N\); the later variation chapter develops these measures further.

Using midpoint values gives

\[\widehat{\bar{x}}=\frac{\sum fm}{N},\qquad\widehat{\sigma^2}=\frac{\sum fm^2}{N}-\widehat{\bar{x}}^{\,2},\qquad\widehat{\sigma}=\sqrt{\widehat{\sigma^2}}.\]

A hat marks an estimate. Variance has squared data units; standard deviation has the original units.
The midpoint model uses \(m=2,6,12\) with frequencies \(4,12,16\). It estimates mean \(8.5\,\mathrm{cm}\) and variance \(\frac{55}{4}\,\mathrm{cm}^2\).

blocks.title: Estimate the mean, variance and standard deviation
blocks.prompt:
Lengths \(x\), in centimetres, have this grouped frequency table.

IntervalFrequency
\(0\le x<2\)\(2\)
\(2\le x<6\)\(3\)
\(6\le x<10\)\(5\)

Use class midpoints to estimate the mean, descriptive variance with divisor \(N\), and standard deviation. Give exact answers.
blocks.hint: The midpoints are \(1,4,8\). Form the columns \(fm\) and \(fm^2\), then divide their totals by the total frequency.
blocks.solution:
1. \[N=10,\quad\sum fm=2(1)+3(4)+5(8)=54.\]
  2. \[\sum fm^2=2(1^2)+3(4^2)+5(8^2)=370.\]
  3. \[\widehat{\bar{x}}=\frac{54}{10}=\frac{27}{5}\,\mathrm{cm}.\]
  4. \[\widehat{\sigma^2}=\frac{370}{10}-\left(\frac{27}{5}\right)^2=\frac{196}{25}\,\mathrm{cm}^2.\]
  5. \[\widehat{\sigma}=\sqrt{\frac{196}{25}}=\frac{14}{5}\,\mathrm{cm}.\]

    All three are estimates because the original positions within each class are unknown.

blocks.html: In \(fm^2\), square the midpoint first, then multiply by frequency: \(fm^2=f(m^2)\), not \((fm)^2\). Use frequencies rather than densities as weights. Keep full intermediate values and round only the final requested answer; a negative variance signals an error or premature rounding.

sections.title: Which answers are estimates, and what information is lost?
sections.label: Partial classes and corrected records
sections.intro: The counts in complete classes are known. A cutoff inside a class needs an additional model: assume observations are distributed uniformly across that class. Then equal fractions of its width represent equal fractions of its frequency.

blocks.html:
\[\text{estimated partial count}=f\times\frac{\text{included width}}{w}.\]

Add all complete classes and the required part of the crossing class. State the uniformity assumption. The result is an estimate and need not be a whole number.

blocks.title: Identify what a correction changes
blocks.prompt:
There are \(25\) measured lengths \(x\), in centimetres.

IntervalFrequency
\(0\le x<6\)\(5\)
\(6\le x<10\)\(8\)
\(10\le x<18\)\(12\)

Assuming a uniform distribution within each class, estimate the number with \(x<14\). An original record of \(11\,\mathrm{cm}\) is then corrected to \(17\,\mathrm{cm}\). Find the increase in the exact raw-data mean, and decide whether the midpoint estimates change.

fields.label: Increase in the exact raw-data mean (cm)
Effect on midpoint mean and variance

blocks.hint: Include two whole classes and half of the last class. The correction changes the raw total, but does it change either class frequency?
blocks.solution:
1. \[\text{estimated count}=5+8+\frac{14-10}{18-10}(12)=19.\]
  2. \[\text{increase in raw mean}=\frac{17-11}{25}=\frac{6}{25}\,\mathrm{cm}.\]

  3. Both records belong to \(10\le x<18\), so the frequencies and midpoint estimates remain unchanged. The grouped estimate below \(14\) also remains \(19\), even though the actual number below \(14\) decreases by one.

blocks.html: Grouping keeps the class counts but loses each original position within a class. Midpoint summaries are estimates, and their errors have no guaranteed direction. If a correction moves a record into a different class, update both affected frequencies and recalculate. If it stays inside its class, the histogram and midpoint estimates remain unchanged even though exact raw-data summaries may change.

glossary.definition: An endpoint of an interval for the original measured variable, rather than merely a rounded label.
The upper class boundary minus the lower class boundary.
The number of observations belonging to a class.
The frequency divided by class width, \(d=\frac{f}{w}\); it supplies a histogram’s height on a density scale.
The average of a class’s two boundaries, used as a representative value in grouped calculations.
A mean that counts each representative value according to how many observations it represents.
The average squared distance from the data mean, using the number of observations \(N\) as divisor.
The square root of variance, expressed in the same units as the data.
An assumption that equal portions of class width contain equal proportions of its observations, used for partial-class estimates.
A value calculated using a model for unknown positions inside classes; it need not equal the summary from the original records.

examples.title: Turn recorded limits into continuous boundaries
examples.question:
Measurements are rounded, with an exact halfway value rounded upwards. Find boundaries and widths for:

(a) lengths rounded to the nearest centimetre, with recorded classes \(10\) through \(14\) and \(15\) through \(19\);

(b) lengths rounded to the nearest \(0.1\,\mathrm{cm}\), with recorded classes \(2.0\) through \(2.4\) and \(2.5\) through \(2.9\).
solution:
(a) Half the precision is \(0.5\,\mathrm{cm}\). The first recorded class represents

\[9.5\le x<14.5.\]

The next represents \(14.5\le x<19.5\). A true value of \(14.5\) rounds to \(15\), so it belongs to the second class.

\[w=14.5-9.5=5\,\mathrm{cm}\]

for the first class, and the second also has width \(5\,\mathrm{cm}\).

(b) Half the precision is \(0.05\,\mathrm{cm}\). The intervals are

\[1.95\le x<2.45,\qquad2.45\le x<2.95.\]

\[w=2.45-1.95=0.5\,\mathrm{cm}.\]

Both classes have this width. The adjustment follows the measurement precision; it is not always half a whole unit.

examples.title: Use area when classes have different widths
examples.question:
The heights of \(32\) plants are grouped using the stated continuous boundaries.

Height \(h\), in cmFrequency \(f\)
\(0\le h<4\)\(4\)
\(4\le h<8\)\(12\)
\(8\le h<16\)\(16\)

Calculate the histogram heights. Identify the class with greatest density and the class containing the most plants.
solution:
Calculate each width from its boundaries, then divide that class’s frequency by its width.

Height, in cm\(f\)Width \(w\)Density \(d=\frac{f}{w}\)
\(0\le h<4\)\(4\)\(4\)\(1\)
\(4\le h<8\)\(12\)\(4\)\(3\)
\(8\le h<16\)\(16\)\(8\)\(2\)
Draw adjacent bars over the intervals with heights \(1,3,2\). Label the horizontal axis “Plant height, cm” and the vertical axis “Frequency density, plants per cm”.

\[4(1)=4,\qquad4(3)=12,\qquad8(2)=16.\]

The three bar areas recover the three frequencies.
The middle class, \(4\le h<8\), has greatest density and the tallest bar. The final class, \(8\le h<16\), contains the most plants because its frequency is \(16\).

examples.title: Read both drawing scales before finding a frequency
examples.question: A histogram for the plant heights uses \(1\,\mathrm{cm}\) on paper for \(2\,\mathrm{cm}\) of plant height. The class \(4\le h<8\) contains \(12\) plants and its paper bar height is \(1.5\,\mathrm{cm}\). Find the vertical scale. The \(8\le h<16\) bar is \(1\,\mathrm{cm}\) tall on paper; use the scale to recover its frequency.
solution:
The known class has data width \(4\,\mathrm{cm}\), so its density is

\[d=\frac{12}{4}=3\text{ plants per cm}.\]

Its paper height is \(1.5\,\mathrm{cm}\). Therefore each vertical centimetre represents

\[\frac{3}{1.5}=2\text{ density units}.\]

The final bar represents density \(1(2)=2\), and its data width is \(16-8=8\). Hence

\[f=8(2)=16.\]

Alternatively, the first paper bar is \(2\,\mathrm{cm}\) wide and \(1.5\,\mathrm{cm}\) tall: area \(3\,\mathrm{cm}^2\) represents \(12\) plants. Thus one paper square centimetre represents \(4\) plants. The final bar has paper area \(4(1)=4\,\mathrm{cm}^2\), representing \(16\) plants.

examples.title: Build the midpoint calculation one column at a time
examples.question:
Estimate the mean, descriptive variance and standard deviation of the \(32\) plant heights. Use divisor \(N\) for variance.

Height \(h\), in cmFrequency \(f\)
\(0\le h<4\)\(4\)
\(4\le h<8\)\(12\)
\(8\le h<16\)\(16\)
solution:
Replace the unknown heights in each class by its midpoint. The final class, for example, has midpoint \(\frac{8+16}{2}=12\). Calculate \(fm\) and \(fm^2\):

Height, in cm\(f\)\(m\)\(fm\)\(fm^2\)
\(0\le h<4\)\(4\)\(2\)\(8\)\(16\)
\(4\le h<8\)\(12\)\(6\)\(72\)\(432\)
\(8\le h<16\)\(16\)\(12\)\(192\)\(2304\)
Total\(32\)\(272\)\(2752\)
\[\widehat{\bar{x}}=\frac{272}{32}=8.5\,\mathrm{cm}.\]

The mean of the squared midpoint values is

\[\frac{\sum fm^2}{N}=\frac{2752}{32}=86\,\mathrm{cm}^2.\]
\[\widehat{\sigma^2}=86-8.5^2=\frac{55}{4}\,\mathrm{cm}^2.\]

\[\widehat{\sigma}=\sqrt{\frac{55}{4}}=\frac{\sqrt{55}}{2}\,\mathrm{cm}.\]

The mean and standard deviation use centimetres; the variance uses square centimetres. None requires an assumption that the actual records equal their midpoints.

examples.title: Separate a grouped estimate from the original records
examples.question:
For the \(32\) plant heights below, estimate how many plants are shorter than \(10\,\mathrm{cm}\), assuming a uniform distribution within each class.

Height \(h\), in cmFrequency \(f\)
\(0\le h<4\)\(4\)
\(4\le h<8\)\(12\)
\(8\le h<16\)\(16\)

One original height of \(9\,\mathrm{cm}\) is then corrected to \(15\,\mathrm{cm}\). Explain the effect on the histogram, midpoint estimates and exact raw-data mean.
solution:
The first two classes contribute all \(4+12=16\) plants. In the final class, the included width is \(10-8=2\) out of \(16-8=8\):

\[\text{estimated count}=4+12+\frac{2}{8}(16)=20.\]

The correction stays within \(8\le h<16\). Every class frequency is unchanged, so the histogram, estimated mean \(8.5\,\mathrm{cm}\) and estimated variance \(\frac{55}{4}\,\mathrm{cm}^2\) stay unchanged.

The raw total increases by \(15-9=6\,\mathrm{cm}\), with the same count \(32\). Therefore the exact mean increases by

\[\frac{6}{32}=\frac{3}{16}\,\mathrm{cm}.\]
The actual number shorter than \(10\,\mathrm{cm}\) decreases by one, while the grouped estimate remains \(20\). The grouped table cannot identify the original positions within the last class.

extraPractice.title: Largest area and tallest bar answer different questions
extraPractice.prompt:
A continuous variable has this grouped frequency table. Calculate each frequency density and identify the class containing the most observations.

ClassFrequency
\(0\le x<4\)12
\(4\le x<12\)20
\(12\le x<18\)18

retry.feedback: Frequency is the bar area. Divide 20 by the class width 8 to obtain its height.

extraPractice.hint: Calculate each class width before dividing frequency by width. Compare areas when comparing frequencies.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[w_1=4,\quad w_2=8,\quad w_3=6.\]
  2. \[d_1=\frac{12}{4}=3,\quad d_2=\frac{20}{8}=\frac{5}{2},\quad d_3=\frac{18}{6}=3.\]

  3. The middle class has the largest frequency, \(20\), despite its lower bar height. The first and third bars have equal heights but unequal areas and frequencies.

extraPractice.title: Adjust rounded measurements, not an explicit interval
extraPractice.prompt: Masses are recorded to the nearest \(0.1\) g, using half-up rounding. A class includes recorded masses from \(5.0\) g through \(5.9\) g. Find its continuous lower boundary, upper boundary and width. A separate table explicitly defines a class by \(10\le x<20\). Should those stated boundaries also receive a rounding adjustment?

options.no: No: use its stated boundaries, 10 and 20.
options.yes: Yes: automatically subtract and add half a unit.

extraPractice.hint: Half the recording precision is \(0.05\) g. Ask whether the table gives rounded recorded labels or already gives continuous boundaries.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[5.0-0.05=4.95,\qquad5.9+0.05=5.95.\]

  2. The class of true masses is \(4.95\le m<5.95\) g under the stated rounding convention, with width \(1\) g.

  3. The interval \(10\le x<20\) already specifies boundaries. Its width is \(10\); a second adjustment would change the question.

extraPractice.title: Convert a physical height using its vertical scale
extraPractice.prompt: A histogram bar covers a class of width \(8\) data units and is \(4\) cm high on paper. Each vertical centimetre represents \(3\) frequency-density units. Horizontally, \(1\) cm represents \(2\) data units. Find the frequency density, frequency and physical bar area in square centimetres.
extraPractice.hint: Convert the paper height to density. For the physical area, also convert the class width to a paper width.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[d=4\times3=12,\qquad f=8\times12=96.\]
  2. \[\text{Paper width}=\frac{8}{2}=4\ \text{cm},\qquad\text{paper area}=4\times4=16\ \text{cm}^{2}.\]

  3. Each square centimetre represents \(2\times3=6\) observations. Thus \(16\times6=96\), confirming the same frequency. A physical area is not itself a frequency until the scale is applied.

extraPractice.title: Estimate the mean, variance and standard deviation
extraPractice.prompt:
Ten lengths, in centimetres, are grouped below. Use class midpoints to estimate the mean, descriptive variance and standard deviation. Give exact numerical answers; use divisor \(N=10\) for the variance.

ClassFrequency
\(0\le x<4\)3
\(4\le x<10\)4
\(10\le x<16\)3
extraPractice.hint: Use midpoints \(2,7,13\). Find \(\sum fm\) and \(\sum fm^2\), then subtract the square of the estimated mean.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[N=10,\quad\sum fm=3(2)+4(7)+3(13)=73.\]
  2. \[\sum fm^2=3(2^2)+4(7^2)+3(13^2)=715.\]
  3. \[\widehat{\bar{x}}=\frac{73}{10}\ \text{cm},\quad\widehat{\sigma^2}=\frac{715}{10}-\left(\frac{73}{10}\right)^2=\frac{1821}{100}\ \text{cm}^{2}.\]
  4. \[\widehat{\sigma}=\frac{\sqrt{1821}}{10}\ \text{cm}.\]

  5. These are exact calculations for the midpoint model, but estimates of the raw-data statistics. The true individual positions within each class are unknown.

extraPractice.title: A partial class needs an explicit assumption
extraPractice.prompt:
Completion times \(t\), in minutes, are grouped as follows. Assuming a uniform distribution within each class, estimate the number completing in less than \(22\) min and the fraction of the sample this represents.

ClassFrequency
\(0\le t<10\)8
\(10\le t<30\)20
\(30\le t<40\)12

fields.label: Is the count determined exactly by this table?

options.no: No: the within-class positions are unknown.
options.yes: Yes: the density makes every partial-class count exact.

extraPractice.hint: Include the whole first class and the first \(12\) minutes of the width-\(20\) middle class.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[\widehat{n}_{t<22}=8+\frac{22-10}{30-10}\times20=20.\]
  2. \[N=8+20+12=40,\qquad\widehat{p} =\frac{20}{40}=\frac{1}{2}.\]

  3. The table gives exact whole-class counts. The partial-class count is an estimate based on spreading the middle-class observations uniformly over its interval.

starters.title: Calibrate the scale, then interpret the histogram
starters.question:
A histogram of \(t\), the completion time in minutes, has these class boundaries and measured paper heights. The first class contains \(12\) observations. All bars use the same vertical scale.

ClassPaper height
\(0\le t<10\)\(1.5\) cm
\(10\le t<25\)\(2\) cm
\(25\le t<35\)\(3\) cm

Find the density units represented by one vertical centimetre, the two missing frequencies, and the midpoint estimate of the mean. Assuming uniformity within each class, estimate the fraction taking more than \(30\) min.
starters.hint: Calibrate from the first bar using its frequency and class width. Apply the same vertical conversion to every height, but use each bar’s own class width.
starters.solution:
1. \[d_1=\frac{12}{10}=1.2,\qquad k=\frac{1.2}{1.5}=\frac{4}{5}.\]
  2. \[f_2=15\left(2\times\frac{4}{5}\right)=24,\quad f_3=10\left(3\times\frac{4}{5}\right)=24,\quad N=60.\]

  3. The second and third bars have equal areas and frequencies, although the third is taller.

  4. \[\widehat{\bar{t}}=\frac{12(5)+24(17.5)+24(30)}{60}=20\ \text{min}.\]
  5. \[\widehat{n}_{t>30}=\frac{35-30}{35-25}(24)=12,\qquad\widehat{p}=\frac{12}{60}=\frac{1}{5}.\]

  6. The mean uses midpoint representatives and the final fraction uses uniformity within a class. Neither reconstructs the exact original times.

  • 1 mark: obtain the common vertical scale.
  • 1 mark: obtain the second frequency using its class width.
  • 1 mark: obtain the third frequency and total.
  • 1 mark: use the correct midpoints and weighted total.
  • 1 mark: obtain the estimated mean with units.

starters.title: A corrected record can leave the grouped table unchanged
starters.question: Six lengths in centimetres were recorded as \(2,7,11,14,19,26\). The value \(11\) was an error and is corrected to \(18\). The grouped classes are \(0\le x<10\), \(10\le x<20\) and \(20\le x<30\). Find the corrected exact mean and descriptive variance. Then find the mean and variance estimated from the grouped midpoint model. State whether the grouped table changes. Use divisor six for both variance calculations.
starters.hint: Recalculate the raw total and sum of squares after replacement. For the grouped calculation, only class membership matters.
starters.solution:
1. The corrected records are \(2,7,18,14,19,26\), with total \(86\) and sum of squares \(1610\).

  2. \[\bar{x}=\frac{86}{6}=\frac{43}{3}\ \text{cm},\qquad\sigma^2=\frac{1610}{6}-\left(\frac{43}{3}\right)^2=\frac{566}{9}\ \text{cm}^{2}.\]

  3. Both \(11\) and \(18\) lie in the middle class. Frequencies remain \(2,3,1\), with midpoints \(5,15,25\).

  4. \[\sum fm=2(5)+3(15)+25=80,\quad\sum fm^2=2(5^2)+3(15^2)+25^2=1350.\]
  5. \[\widehat{\bar{x}}=\frac{40}{3}\ \text{cm},\qquad\widehat{\sigma^2}=\frac{1350}{6}-\left(\frac{40}{3}\right)^2=\frac{425}{9}\ \text{cm}^{2}.\]

  6. The histogram and midpoint estimates are unchanged. Grouping has discarded the within-class position that this correction changes; an unchanged histogram does not imply unchanged raw-data statistics.
